strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: reusing 'sunk' compute from smaller pretrained checkpoints to build larger models, with direct relevance to reducing LLM pretraining costs.

The interpositional vs. stacking layer-growth comparison is well motivated by an interesting empirical observation (characteristic layer-wise weight-norm trend across many converged models, both self-trained and popular open-source MoE models such as DeepSeek-V2, Qwen3, Mixtral, Hunyuan, dots.llm1, GroveMoE), lending some generality to the hypothesis.
The work is validated at genuinely large scale (17B -> 35B -> 70B, over 1T tokens), which is a substantial engineering effort rarely seen in growth-method papers that typically stay at small scale.

A reasonably systematic set of ablations is provided: depth vs width growth trade-offs, noise-injection scale for expert duplication, pre-norm vs post-norm stability analysis, and a dedicated study of growth timing relative to sunk cost.
Extensive appendix with full per-checkpoint evaluation tables, architecture/hyperparameter details, and dataset composition supports reproducibility of the reported numbers.

The finding that growth timing/sunk cost correlates with final performance, together with the heuristic that additional FLOPs should be on the same order as sunk cost, offers a practically useful guideline for practitioners deciding when to grow a checkpoint.
weaknesses: A critical baseline is missing: the paper never compares growing a checkpoint against simply continuing to train the *original, non-grown* model for the same extra FLOPs. Without this, it is unclear how much of the 'benefit of sunk cost' is due to growth itself versus the trivial fact that later checkpoints already have higher accuracy before any additional training (as shown by the 'Start acc' column in Table 1). This weakens the central claim that growth is the mechanism unlocking the sunk-cost value.

Nearly all quantitative claims (10.66% gain, 1% noise-injection improvement, sunk-cost correlations) appear to be based on single training runs per configuration at each scale, with no repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing—particularly concerning for small differences (e.g., ~1% accuracy gaps from noise level) and for the headline 70B result, which rests on one run per condition.

The core contribution is largely an empirical/engineering study rather than a new algorithmic idea: interpositional layer duplication and expert duplication with small Gaussian noise are incremental variations on existing stacking/upcycling techniques; the theoretical justification (weight-norm trend argument) is heuristic rather than rigorously connected to the function-preserving principle invoked in the paper.

No direct quantitative comparison to competing growth/upcycling baselines from the literature (e.g., LLaMA Pro block expansion, Sparse Upcycling, Drop-Upcycling, LEMON/LiGO) is provided beyond the authors' own stack-vs-interposition ablation, making it hard to judge how much better this framework is relative to prior art.

The learning-rate confound noted by the authors themselves (same constant LR used for all continued-training runs regardless of the checkpoint's position in its original schedule) likely biases results against late-checkpoint growth and complicates interpretation of the timing study.

Generalization is only demonstrated within one proprietary training pipeline/architecture family; while weight-norm patterns are shown for external models, no external model is actually grown and retrained to validate the method beyond the authors' own models.

strengths: Large-scale empirical validation is rare and valuable: the paper scales its method to a 70B-parameter MoE model trained on 1T tokens, going well beyond the small-scale toy settings common in prior model-growth literature.

Systematic and well-designed ablations: the paper carefully isolates variables (growth factor k, noise scale for width growth, routing variants such as fixed E with variable top-k), and each ablation is backed by quantitative loss/accuracy curves.

The identification of a 'convergence boundary' (~1x Chinchilla-optimal FLOPs) at which interpositional growth begins to outperform stacking is a concrete, testable, and novel practical finding, supported by both loss/accuracy curves and correlated weight-norm analysis (Figure 4, 5, Table 1).

Thorough orthogonality analysis (Appendix E) using Adam first-moment cosine similarity, cumulative weight-delta divergence, and order-independence experiments at 12B scale, providing multiple corroborating pieces of evidence rather than a single metric.

The sunk-cost timing study (Section 4) is a genuinely useful practical contribution for practitioners deciding whether/when to grow an existing checkpoint, including guidance on matching additional FLOPs to sunk FLOPs magnitude.

Extensive documentation of hyperparameters, architecture, dataset composition, and full per-checkpoint evaluation tables in the appendix, which aids partial reproducibility despite proprietary training infrastructure.
weaknesses: Central large-scale results (70B model, 10.6% improvement claim) rest on single training runs without seeds/error bars, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains are statistically robust rather than run-to-run noise, especially given the very large investment required to repeat such experiments.

The scratch-training baseline used for the headline 10.6% comparison is not clearly shown to be equally well-tuned (e.g., learning-rate schedule, warmup) as the grown model's continued-training regime; differences in optimization setup could partially explain the gap rather than the growth technique alone.

No direct empirical comparison against existing model growth/upcycling baselines (e.g., LLaMA Pro-style stacking at comparable MoE scale, Komatsuzaki et al. sparse upcycling, or Liew et al. 2025 upcycling scaling laws) under matched compute budgets; comparisons to these methods are only discussed qualitatively in related work.

The theoretical grounding connecting the weight-norm monotonic pattern to 'healthy convergence' and to why interposition specifically preserves it is largely qualitative/heuristic, leaning on loosely related theoretical results (neural ODE regularization, DeepNet stability) without a rigorous derivation specific to the claimed phenomenon.

All experiments use a single proprietary architecture, tokenizer, and data mixture; generalizability of findings (e.g., noise-scale sensitivity, depth-vs-width growth trade-off) to other MoE designs (different routing, granularity, or expert-choice routing) is not empirically tested, only weight-norm patterns are checked against a few public checkpoints.

Data, code, and model checkpoints do not appear to be released, and the training corpus mixes proprietary/synthetic data, limiting the ability of the community to reproduce the large-scale results even in principle.

The 'sunk cost' framing, while a nice narrative device, mostly formalizes an intuitive expectation (models trained longer/more make better initializations); the paper's novel technical contribution is more precisely the two specific growth operators (interposition, noisy expert duplication) rather than the sunk-cost concept itself.
